claim: The human cortex is characterized by local morphological features such as cortical thickness, myelin content, and gene expression that change along the posterior-anterior axis.
source: The human cortex is characterized by local morphological features such as cortical thickness, myelin content, and gene expression that change along the posterior-anterior axis.
evidence: This is a general statement about cortical organization that draws from established scientific knowledge about brain structure.

claim: In resting-state MEG recordings from 187 healthy participants, the dominant peak frequency in a brain area decreases significantly along the posterior-anterior axis following the global hierarchy from early sensory to higher order areas.
source: In resting-state MEG recordings from healthy participants (N = 187) using mixed effect models, we found that the dominant peak frequency in a brain area decreases significantly along the posterior-anterior axis following the global hierarchy from early sensory to higher order areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental MEG data from 187 participants analyzed using mixed effect models.

claim: The spatial gradient of peak frequency was significantly anticorrelated with that of cortical thickness.
source: This spatial gradient of peak frequency was significantly anticorrelated with that of cortical thickness, representing a proxy of the cortical hierarchical level.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the relationship between measured peak frequency and cortical thickness data.

claim: Cortical thickness represents a proxy of the cortical hierarchical level.
source: This spatial gradient of peak frequency was significantly anticorrelated with that of cortical thickness, representing a proxy of the cortical hierarchical level.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cortical thickness as an indicator of hierarchical organization.

claim: The dominant frequency changes systematically and globally along the spatial and hierarchical gradients.
source: This result indicates that the dominant frequency changes systematically and globally along the spatial and hierarchical gradients and establishes a new structure-function relationship pertaining to brain oscillations as a core organization that may underlie hierarchical specialization in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing the relationship between frequency, spatial location, and cortical thickness.

claim: The frequency gradient establishes a new structure-function relationship pertaining to brain oscillations that may underlie hierarchical specialization in the brain.
source: This result indicates that the dominant frequency changes systematically and globally along the spatial and hierarchical gradients and establishes a new structure-function relationship pertaining to brain oscillations as a core organization that may underlie hierarchical specialization in the brain.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings regarding the functional significance of the observed gradient.

claim: Many structural features that distinguish individual brain areas change gradually in an orderly manner across the cortex, leading to spatial feature gradients.
source: Interestingly, many structural features that distinguish individual brain areas change gradually in an orderly manner across the cortex, leading to spatial feature gradients.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous anatomical studies.

claim: The most prominent and best established gradients are evident along the posterior-anterior axis.
source: The most prominent and best established gradients are evident along the posterior-anterior axis (Eickhoff et al., 2018; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Huntenburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neuron density decreases from posterior to anterior brain areas.
source: For instance, neuron density decreases and neuronal connectivity increases from posterior to anterior brain areas.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Neuronal connectivity increases from posterior to anterior brain areas.
source: For instance, neuron density decreases and neuronal connectivity increases from posterior to anterior brain areas.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Differences in neuron density and connectivity have been attributed to differences in neurogenesis for posterior compared to anterior brain areas.
source: These differences have been attributed to differences in neurogenesis for posterior compared to anterior brain areas (Hill et al., 2010; Huntenburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A similar posterior-anterior gradient has been observed for myelin content, cortical thickness, and gene expression.
source: A similar posterior-anterior gradient has been observed for myelin content, cortical thickness, and gene expression (Burt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Huntenburg et al. suggest a sensorimotor to transmodal gradient as an important intrinsic organizing dimension of human cortex.
source: For instance, Huntenburg et al. suggest a sensorimotor to transmodal gradient as an important intrinsic organizing dimension of human cortex (Huntenburg et al., 2018) reflecting gradual changes in structural features from functionally unimodal (dedicated sensory or motor) areas to higher order, transmodal areas.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Cortical areas are structurally connected into larger networks, which often display a hierarchical organization.
source: In addition to structural gradients as an organizing principle reflecting global cortical organization, it is well acknowledged that cortical areas are structurally connected into larger networks, which often display a hierarchical organization.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about brain organization.

claim: Cortical hierarchies are typically established based on the degree of microstructural differentiation of the connected areas, and on the classification of the anatomical connections as feedforward or feedback using histological tract-tracing.
source: Cortical hierarchies are typically established based on the degree of microstructural differentiation of the connected areas, and on the classification of the anatomical connections as feedforward or feedback using histological tract-tracing.
evidence: This describes established methods for determining cortical hierarchies.

claim: Early sensory areas with predominantly feedforward outgoing connections are placed at the bottom of the hierarchy and higher order association areas with mostly feedback outgoing connections are placed at the top of the hierarchy.
source: Early sensory areas with predominantly feedforward outgoing connections are placed at the bottom of the hierarchy and higher order association areas with mostly feedback outgoing connections are placed at the top of the hierarchy (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Markov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on cortical hierarchies.

claim: Cortical thickness is a noninvasive, but indirect index of cortical hierarchies.
source: A noninvasive, but indirect index of these hierarchies is cortical thickness, a macroscopic feature of the cortex, which can be estimated from MRI scans.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cortical thickness as a measure.

claim: Cortical thickness mirrors global hierarchical organization of the cortex as well as local hierarchies in visual, auditory and somatosensory areas.
source: It has been shown that cortical thickness mirrors global hierarchical organization of the cortex as well as local hierarchies in visual, auditory and somatosensory areas (Jasmin et al., 2019; Wagstyl et al., 2015), and, therefore, could be used as a basis for understanding hierarchy-gradient relationships in the cortex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cortical areas follow a hierarchical ordering in their timescales of intrinsic fluctuations as measured in the autocorrelation of spiking activity.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that cortical areas follow a hierarchical ordering in their timescales of intrinsic fluctuations as for example measured in the autocorrelation of spiking activity (Murray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Sensory areas show faster fluctuations while frontal areas show slower fluctuations.
source: Sensory areas show faster fluctuations while frontal areas show slower fluctuations.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about temporal dynamics in different brain areas.

claim: Shorter timescales in sensory areas enable them to reflect dynamic changes in the environment, whereas the longer timescales in prefrontal areas allow for integration of information.
source: Shorter timescales in sensory areas enables them to reflect dynamic changes in the environment, whereas the longer timescales in prefrontal areas allows for integration of information.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of different timescales.

claim: The gradient of 'temporal receptive windows' has been demonstrated in visual and auditory processing.
source: Particularly, this gradient of 'temporal receptive windows' has been demonstrated in visual (Himberger et al., 2018) and auditory processing (Jasmin et al., 2019) and could be related to the frequency of spontaneous brain oscillations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Oscillations are a prominent feature of brain activity, and have been suggested to play a central role in coordinating neuronal activity.
source: Oscillations are a prominent feature of brain activity, and have been suggested to play a central role in coordinating neuronal activity (Fries, 2005; Wang, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The spectral activity patterns have been shown to be characteristic for each brain area.
source: Similar to many anatomical features described above, the spectral activity patterns have been shown to be characteristic for each brain area (Keitel and Gross, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The individual anatomical structure of a brain area shapes its rhythmic neuronal activity.
source: This is consistent with the view that the individual anatomical structure of a brain area shapes its rhythmic neuronal activity, which led us to hypothesize the existence of a posterior-anterior gradient in the frequency of spontaneous brain rhythms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between structure and function.

claim: MEG studies revealed strongest cortical generators for the dominant alpha rhythm (7–13 Hz) in occipito-parietal brain areas.
source: Overall, these MEG studies revealed strongest cortical generators for the dominant alpha rhythm (7–13 Hz) in occipito-parietal brain areas.
evidence: This is based on previous MEG studies.

claim: The beta band (15–30 Hz) shows strongest activity in sensorimotor areas.
source: The beta band (15–30 Hz) shows strongest activity in sensorimotor areas while delta (1–3 Hz) and theta (3–7 Hz) bands are associated with activity in wide-spread areas including frontal cortex.
evidence: This is based on previous MEG studies.

claim: Delta (1–3 Hz) and theta (3–7 Hz) bands are associated with activity in wide-spread areas including frontal cortex.
source: The beta band (15–30 Hz) shows strongest activity in sensorimotor areas while delta (1–3 Hz) and theta (3–7 Hz) bands are associated with activity in wide-spread areas including frontal cortex.
evidence: This is based on previous MEG studies.

claim: There is a significant correlation (r = −0.84, p<<0.001) between the trimmed mean PF and the ROI's y-coordinate.
source: A clear gradual decrease of PF from posterior to anterior is evident and supported by a significant correlation (skipped Pearson correlation, Robust Correlation Toolbox) (Pernet et al., 2012) between the trimmed mean PF and the ROI's y-coordinate (r = −0.84, p<<0.001).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the MEG data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At the individual level, a significant posterior-to-anterior gradient of PF was found for 84% of participants (p<0.05).
source: At the individual level, we computed the correlation between the Y-coordinates and PF values and found a significant posterior-to-anterior gradient of PF for 84% of participants (p<0.05).
evidence: This is based on individual-level statistical analysis of the MEG data.

claim: LMEM yielded highly significant scores for Y (t = −15.6, p<<0.001), Z (t = −10.4, p<<0.001), and Y:Z (t = −32, p<<0.001) directions.
source: LMEM yielded highly significant scores for Y (t = −15.6, p<<0.001), Z (t = −10.4, p<<0.001), and Y:Z (t = −32, p<<0.001) directions.
evidence: This is based on linear mixed effect modeling of the MEG data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The peak frequency of brain oscillations decreases systematically in posterior-anterior direction.
source: Together, these results support the conclusion that the peak frequency of brain oscillations decreases systematically in posterior-anterior direction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the LMEM results.

claim: LMEM identified a second global axis where PF decreases along the Z axis (inferior-superior direction).
source: Furthermore, LMEM identified a second global axis where PF decreases along the Z axis (inferior-superior direction).
evidence: This is based on the LMEM analysis results.

claim: There is a highly significant negative dependence between PF and geodesic distance from V1 (t = −21.1, p<<0.001) for areas located 2–3 cm away from V1.
source: To address this question, we computed the geodesic distance between the reference ROI, V1, and all areas located 2–3 cm away from V1, and applied linear mixed effect modelling of PF as a function of the distance values. We found a highly significant negative dependence between PF and distance (t = −21.1, p<<0.001).
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis of geodesic distance data.

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between the trimmed mean PF and the geodesic distance values (r = −0.89, p<<0.001).
source: Our analysis showed a significant negative correlation between the trimmed mean PF and the geodesic distance values (r = −0.89, p<<0.001; Figure 1D top-left panel).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of geodesic distance data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: LMEM found a highly significant gradient of PF along the specified geodesic distance (t = −18.9, p<<0.001).
source: To account for this inter-individual variability, we applied an LMEM between the PF as a response variable and the geodesic distance values as an independent variable. We found a highly significant gradient of PF along the specified geodesic distance (t = −18.9, p<<0.001; Figure 1E, cortical map).
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: LMEM found a significant gradient for three consecutive windows along the Y axis (window 1: t = −8.1, window 2: t = −10.9, window 3: t = −5.2, all p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, to answer the question whether the spatial gradient of PF constantly exists in different areas of the cortex, we split the cortex to three equal, consecutive and non-overlapping windows (about 4 cm) based on the Y axis, applied LMEM for each window modelling PF as a function of geodesic distance, and found a significant gradient (window 1: t = −8.1, window 2: t = −10.9, window 3: t = −5.2, all p<0.001) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis of three separate cortical windows shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The spatial gradient of PF along the posterior-anterior direction exists systematically and constantly across all cortical windows.
source: Indeed, our analysis demonstrates a significant organization of PF along the posterior-anterior direction for all windows indicating that this axis constitutes a systematic and constant gradient of PF.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the window-based LMEM analysis.

claim: There is a significant decrease of the 1/f slope along the posterior-to-anterior direction (Y: t = −4.3, p<<0.001).
source: As illustrated in Figure 2A and B, we found significant scores for Y (slope: t = −4.3, p<<0.001; offset: t = 2.8, p<0.01), Y:Z (slope: t = 6.9, p<<0.001; offset: t = 13.2, p<<0.001), and X:Y (slope: t = −6.8, p<<0.001; offset: t = −5.8, p<<0.001) directions.
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis of 1/f slope parameters shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is a significant increase of the 1/f offset along the posterior-to-anterior direction (Y: t = 2.8, p<0.01).
source: As illustrated in Figure 2A and B, we found significant scores for Y (slope: t = −4.3, p<<0.001; offset: t = 2.8, p<0.01), Y:Z (slope: t = 6.9, p<<0.001; offset: t = 13.2, p<<0.001), and X:Y (slope: t = −6.8, p<<0.001; offset: t = −5.8, p<<0.001) directions.
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis of 1/f offset parameters shown in Figure 2.

claim: After regressing out 1/f parameters, there is a significant posterior-anterior gradient of residual PF values (t-values: Y = −8.3, Z = −4.3, Y:Z = −16; all p<<0.001).
source: The results confirmed a significant posterior-anterior gradient of residual PF values (t-values: Y = −8.3, Z = −4.3, Y:Z = −16; all p<<0.001, Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis after regressing out 1/f parameters, shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The posterior-anterior PF gradient is largely independent of the observed gradients of slope and offset of the 1/f component.
source: We therefore conclude that the posterior-anterior PF gradient is largely independent of the observed gradients of slope and offset of the 1/f component.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis showing significant PF gradient after removing 1/f effects.

claim: There is a significant change of mean CT along the posterior-anterior axis (r = 0.36, p<<0.001).
source: Figure 3 shows a significant change of mean CT along the posterior-anterior axis (r = 0.36, p<<0.001, top panel).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of cortical thickness data shown in Figure 3.

claim: LMEM of CT as a function of ROI coordinates showed a significant and progressive increase of CT from posterior to anterior regions (t-values: Y = 49.7, Z = −29.3, Y:Z = 16.2; all p<<0.001).
source: LMEM of CT as a function of ROI coordinates showed a significant and progressive increase of CT from posterior to anterior regions (t-values: Y = 49.7, Z = −29.3, Y:Z = 16.2; all p<<0.001).
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis of cortical thickness data.

claim: LMEM identified a secondary inferior-superior axis of CT.
source: Notably, similar to the spatial gradients of PF, LMEM uncovered a secondary inferior-superior axis of CT.
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis of cortical thickness data.

claim: LMEM showed a significant negative relationship between PF and CT (t = −13.8, p<<0.001).
source: Having established the organizational axes of CT, we then tested for a significant relationship between CT and PF. LMEM (t = −13.8, p<<0.001) showed a significant negative relationship between PF and CT.
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis of the relationship between PF and CT.

claim: PFres and CTres are significantly related (LMEM: t = −6.9, p<<0.001) after removing the effect of ROI coordinates.
source: PFres and CTres are still significantly related (LMEM: t = −6.9, p<<0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) indicating that they are more directly related to each other than can be explained by their individual dependency on location (x,y,z).
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis of residual values shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Peak frequency is related to structural features that likely represent cortical hierarchies.
source: This result suggests that peak frequency is related to structural features that likely represent cortical hierarchies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the relationship between PF and CT after removing spatial effects.

claim: There is a significant decrease of PF along the visual hierarchy (t = −10.1, p<<0.001).
source: We modeled spatial changes of PF along the visual hierarchy, using LMEM (see Materials and method section for details), and found a significant decrease of PF (t = −10.1, p<<0.001).
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis of seven visual areas shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a significant increase of CT along the visual hierarchy (t = 54.9, p<<0.001).
source: A similar analysis was also performed on CT and found a significant increase of CT along the visual hierarchy (t = 54.9, p<<0.001).
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis of seven visual areas shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Markers of hierarchical microcircuit specialization such as the ratio of T1-weighted to T2-weighted MRI maps (T1w/T2w) are significantly different between sensory and association areas.
source: Markers of hierarchical microcircuit specialization such as the ratio of T1-weighted to T2-weighted MRI maps (T1w/T2w) are significantly different between sensory and association areas (Burt et al., 2018; Demirtaş et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is a significant effect of resting-state networks on PF (F-stats = 264, p<<0.001).
source: Next, we applied ANOVA on LMEM and found a significant effect of resting-state networks for PF and CT (PF: F-stats = 264, p<<0.001; CT: F-stats = 746, p<<0.001).
evidence: This is based on ANOVA analysis of LMEM shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There is a significant effect of resting-state networks on CT (F-stats = 746, p<<0.001).
source: Next, we applied ANOVA on LMEM and found a significant effect of resting-state networks for PF and CT (PF: F-stats = 264, p<<0.001; CT: F-stats = 746, p<<0.001).
evidence: This is based on ANOVA analysis of LMEM shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PF is significantly lower in association RSNs (except for DAN) than in sensory RSNs (t = −11.1, p<<0.001).
source: Similarly, PF and CT were significantly different between sensory and association areas (LMEM, PF: t = −11.1, p<<0.001; CT: t = 14.7, p<<0.001, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis comparing sensory and association networks shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CT is significantly higher in association RSNs than in sensory RSNs (t = 14.7, p<<0.001).
source: Similarly, PF and CT were significantly different between sensory and association areas (LMEM, PF: t = −11.1, p<<0.001; CT: t = 14.7, p<<0.001, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis comparing sensory and association networks shown in Figure 4B.

claim: After regressing out the effect of spatial location, a significant difference among networks remained for PF.
source: However, we also tested if PF and CT differ between networks irrespective of their location. This was done by removing from both measures changes that can be explained by linear dependencies on x,y,z. Interestingly, after regressing out the effect of spatial location, a significant difference among networks remained for PF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and CT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis after removing spatial effects, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: After regressing out the effect of spatial location, a significant difference among networks remained for CT.
source: However, we also tested if PF and CT differ between networks irrespective of their location. This was done by removing from both measures changes that can be explained by linear dependencies on x,y,z. Interestingly, after regressing out the effect of spatial location, a significant difference among networks remained for PF (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and CT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis after removing spatial effects, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Beyond a global effect of location, networks still differ significantly in PF and CT after removing the linear effects of location.
source: These results indicate that, beyond a global effect of location, networks still differ significantly in PF and CT after removing the linear effects of location.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of location-independent network differences.

claim: The histogram of peak frequencies delineates the classical frequency bands: theta (4–7.5 Hz), alpha (8.5–13 Hz), low beta (15–25 Hz), and high beta (27.5–34 Hz).
source: Interestingly, this histogram of peak frequencies clearly delineates the classical frequency bands that are traditionally used in the EEG and MEG literature – but they are here derived in a purely data-driven manner (4–7.5 Hz (theta), 8.5–13 Hz (alpha), 15–25 Hz (low beta) 27.5–34 Hz (high beta), for subsequent analysis both beta bands were combined).
evidence: This is based on data-driven analysis of the histogram shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is a significant decrease of alpha peak frequency along the posterior-anterior direction (correlation with y-axis: r = -0.87, p<<0.001; LMEM: Y, t = −10, p<<0.001; Y:Z, t = 3.2, p=0.001).
source: We found a significant decrease of alpha peak frequency (correlation with y-axis: r = - 0.87, p<<0.001; LMEM: Y, t = −10, p<<0.001;=Y:Z, t = 3.2, p=0.001, Figure 6B and E) only along the posterior-anterior direction, while theta- (correlation with y-axis: r = 0.40, p<0.001; LMEM: Y, t = 7.4, p<<0.0.001; Z, t = −7, p<<0.001; Y:Z, t = −8, p<<0.001, Figure 6A and D) and beta-range (correlation with y-axis: r = 0.9, p<<0.001; LMEM: Y, t = 9.3, p<<0.001; Z, t = 4.7, p<<0.001; Y:Z, t = 2.3, p<<0.001, Figure 6C and F) frequencies significantly increased along the same direction.
evidence: This is based on correlation and LMEM analysis of alpha band data shown in Figure 6B and E.

claim: Theta-range frequencies significantly increased along the posterior-anterior direction (correlation with y-axis: r = 0.40, p<0.001; LMEM: Y, t = 7.4, p<<0.001; Z, t = −7, p<<0.001; Y:Z, t = −8, p<<0.001).
source: We found a significant decrease of alpha peak frequency (correlation with y-axis: r = - 0.87, p<<0.001; LMEM: Y, t = −10, p<<0.001;=Y:Z, t = 3.2, p=0.001, Figure 6B and E) only along the posterior-anterior direction, while theta- (correlation with y-axis: r = 0.40, p<0.001; LMEM: Y, t = 7.4, p<<0.0.001; Z, t = −7, p<<0.001; Y:Z, t = −8, p<<0.001, Figure 6A and D) and beta-range (correlation with y-axis: r = 0.9, p<<0.001; LMEM: Y, t = 9.3, p<<0.001; Z, t = 4.7, p<<0.001; Y:Z, t = 2.3, p<<0.001, Figure 6C and F) frequencies significantly increased along the same direction.
evidence: This is based on correlation and LMEM analysis of theta band data shown in Figure 6A and D.

claim: Beta-range frequencies significantly increased along the posterior-anterior direction (correlation with y-axis: r = 0.9, p<<0.001; LMEM: Y, t = 9.3, p<<0.001; Z, t = 4.7, p<<0.001; Y:Z, t = 2.3, p<<0.001).
source: We found a significant decrease of alpha peak frequency (correlation with y-axis: r = - 0.87, p<<0.001; LMEM: Y, t = −10, p<<0.001;=Y:Z, t = 3.2, p=0.001, Figure 6B and E) only along the posterior-anterior direction, while theta- (correlation with y-axis: r = 0.40, p<0.001; LMEM: Y, t = 7.4, p<<0.0.001; Z, t = −7, p<<0.001; Y:Z, t = −8, p<<0.001, Figure 6A and D) and beta-range (correlation with y-axis: r = 0.9, p<<0.001; LMEM: Y, t = 9.3, p<<0.001; Z, t = 4.7, p<<0.001; Y:Z, t = 2.3, p<<0.001, Figure 6C and F) frequencies significantly increased along the same direction.
evidence: This is based on correlation and LMEM analysis of beta band data shown in Figure 6C and F.

claim: LMEM identified a secondary significant gradient of theta- and beta-PF along the z-axis.
source: Moreover, LMEM identified a secondary significant gradient of theta- and beta-PF along the z-axis.
evidence: This is based on LMEM analysis of theta and beta band data.

claim: This is the first comprehensive demonstration of frequency gradients across the human cortex using a large set of resting-state MEG recordings.
source: This study is the first comprehensive demonstration of frequency gradients across the human cortex using a large set of resting-state MEG recordings.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The frequency gradient of resting-state brain rhythms complements previous anatomical studies reporting a posterior-anterior gradient in microscale and macroscale anatomical features of animal and human cortex.
source: This finding establishes a frequency gradient of resting-state brain rhythms that complements previous anatomical studies reporting a posterior-anterior gradient in microscale and macroscale anatomical features of animal and human cortex (Huntenburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference about how the current findings relate to previous research, supported by citation.

claim: Several MEG/EEG studies have demonstrated that alpha activity (~10 Hz) is strongest in occipito-parietal brain areas and theta activity (~5 Hz) strongest in more frontal brain areas.
source: Several MEG/EEG studies have demonstrated that alpha activity (~10 Hz) is strongest in occipito-parietal brain areas and theta activity (~5 Hz) strongest in more frontal brain areas (Chiang et al., 2011; Voytek et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is evidence that the dominant frequencies differ between brain areas.
source: There is also evidence that the dominant frequencies differ between brain areas (Groppe et al., 2013; Hillebrand et al., 2016; Keitel and Gross, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: This study provides the first comprehensive (in frequency and space) statistical model of frequency gradients in a large resting-state brain activity dataset.
source: However, we provide the first comprehensive (in frequency and space) statistical model of frequency gradients in a large resting-state brain activity.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and comprehensiveness of the study.

claim: The results are consistent with a recent invasive study showing a systematic decrease of peak frequency from posterior to anterior brain areas in ECoG recordings of epilepsy patients.
source: Our results are consistent with a recent invasive study showing a systematic decrease of peak frequency from posterior to anterior brain areas in ECoG recordings of epilepsy patients (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The observed correlation between PF and CT holds after removing the effect of spatial location (x,y,z).
source: The observed correlation holds after removing the effect of spatial location (x,y,z).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of residual values after removing spatial effects.

claim: PF and CT are more closely related to each other than can be explained by spatial location alone.
source: This seems to indicate that PF and CT are more closely related to each other than can be explained by spatial location alone.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of residual correlations.

claim: Both PF and CT follow cortical hierarchies.
source: Since cortical hierarchies do not strictly follow a single linear trajectory in space (e.g. posterior-anterior) our results are consistent with the idea that both PF and CT, follow cortical hierarchies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the relationship between PF, CT, and spatial location.

claim: Local spatial gradients have been reported in multiple features of cortex during auditory perception and visual processing streams.
source: Indeed, such local spatial gradients have been reported in multiple features of cortex during auditory perception (Jasmin et al., 2019) and visual processing streams (Himberger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Local gradients could mirror complex organization of gradients in human cortex and support the approach of global gradient along the sensory to transmodal areas.
source: From a broader view, local gradients could mirror complex organization of gradients in human cortex and support the approach of global gradient along the sensory to transmodal areas (Huntenburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: The posterior-anterior gradient of PF was significant after subtracting CT scores from PF values, suggesting a partial independence of both measures.
source: On the other hand, posterior-anterior gradient of PF was significant after subtracting CT scores from PF values. This suggests a partial independence of both measures.
evidence: This is based on analysis showing PF gradient remains after removing CT effects.

claim: Since PF is a measure derived from brain activity, the reported gradient could be modulated dynamically depending on cognitive state or task demands.
source: Since PF is a measure derived from brain activity the reported gradient could be modulated dynamically depending on cognitive state or task demands.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential dynamic modulation of the gradient.

claim: Zhang et al. demonstrated the existence of travelling waves along the frequency gradient.
source: Zhang et al. demonstrated the existence of travelling waves along the frequency gradient (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Local frequencies along the posterior-to-anterior direction are positively correlated with waves' propagation speed and direction consistent with a proposed model of travelling waves based on weakly coupled oscillators (WCO).
source: Interestingly, they found that local frequencies along the posterior-to-anterior direction are positively correlated with waves' propagation speed and direction consistent with a proposed model of travelling waves based on weakly coupled oscillators (WCO) (Ermentrout and Kleinfeld, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Travelling waves along the posterior-anterior axis have been reported during visual stimulation.
source: Travelling waves along the posterior-anterior axis have also been reported during visual stimulation (Alamia and VanRullen, 2019; Lozano-Soldevilla and VanRullen, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Travelling waves might serve to drive neural communication along the cortical hierarchy possibly through nested gamma oscillations thereby linking travelling waves to the concept of pulsed inhibition.
source: These travelling waves might serve to drive neural communication along the cortical hierarchy possibly through nested gamma oscillations thereby linking travelling waves to the concept of pulsed inhibition (Bahramisharif et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Travelling waves have been associated with memory consolidation and learning.
source: In addition, travelling waves have been associated with memory consolidation and learning (Muller et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Frequency gradients have been reported previously in the entorhinal cortex.
source: It is of interest to note that frequency gradients have been reported previously in the entorhinal cortex (Giocomo et al., 2011; Giocomo and Hasselmo, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the entorhinal cortex, a frequency decrease and corresponding travelling waves have been observed in the dorsal-ventral direction and have been related to a representational gradient of spatial scales from coarse to fine.
source: Here, a frequency decrease and corresponding travelling waves have been observed in the dorsal-ventral direction and have been related to a representational gradient of spatial scales from coarse to fine (Muller et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Converging evidence across recording methods, species and cortical domains suggests that representations become more 'integrated' with decreasing 'dominant' frequency of the underlying neuronal population.
source: Indeed, converging evidence across recording methods, species and cortical domains suggests that representations become more 'integrated' with decreasing 'dominant' frequency of the underlying neuronal population.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple lines of evidence across different studies.

claim: In the auditory cortex, response latencies and complexity of processing increase along the posterior-anterior axis.
source: A prime example is the auditory cortex where response latencies and complexity of processing increase along the posterior-anterior axis (Jasmin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In the auditory cortex, there is an increase in cortical thickness and increased ratio of feedback to feedforward connections along the posterior-anterior axis.
source: This is also mirrored by an increase in cortical thickness and increased ratio of feedback to feedforward connections along this axis.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about auditory cortex organization.

claim: Timescales of intrinsic fluctuations in spiking activity increase from posterior to anterior brain areas.
source: Similar observations have been made across more widely distributed cortical areas where timescales of intrinsic fluctuations in spiking activity increase from posterior to anterior brain areas (Murray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Time scales of intrinsic fluctuations are largely determined by the time constants of synaptic transmission.
source: Not surprisingly, these time scales are largely determined by the time constants of synaptic transmission (Duarte et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In a computational model of activity in macaque cortex using anatomical connectivity, a gradient of time scales emerges with short, transient responses to input in sensory areas and slower, sustained responses in higher order areas.
source: But interestingly, in a computational model of activity in macaque cortex using anatomical connectivity a gradient of time scales also emerges with short, transient responses to input in sensory areas and slower, sustained responses in higher order areas (Chaudhuri et al., 2015) (see also Kiebel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cortical peak frequencies decrease systematically along the inferior-superior axis.
source: Our approach additionally revealed that cortical peak frequencies decrease systematically along the inferior-superior axis.
evidence: This is based on the LMEM analysis results.

claim: Higher order frontal areas with lower PF have higher z-coordinates compared to the early sensory areas with higher PF.
source: As seen in Figure 1 this seems to result from the fact that higher order frontal areas with lower PF have higher z-coordinates compared to the early sensory areas with higher PF.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spatial distribution shown in Figure 1.

claim: A similar inferior-superior gradient was also observed for cortical thickness.
source: A similar inferior-superior gradient was also observed for cortical thickness.
evidence: This is based on the LMEM analysis results for CT.

claim: A recent study reported an inferior-superior gradient organization of the CT in human and macaque monkeys.
source: This finding is supported by a recent study reporting an inferior-superior gradient organization of the CT in human and macaque monkeys (Valk et al., 2020), and has been attributed to the organization patterns expected based on the theory of dual origin (Goulas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The inferior-superior gradient has been attributed to the organization patterns expected based on the theory of dual origin.
source: This finding is supported by a recent study reporting an inferior-superior gradient organization of the CT in human and macaque monkeys (Valk et al., 2020), and has been attributed to the organization patterns expected based on the theory of dual origin (Goulas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: This is the first MEG study to identify frequency bands from peak frequencies in a large data set.
source: This is the first MEG study to our knowledge to identify frequency bands from peak frequencies in a large data set (see Groppe et al., 2013 for a similar approach in a smaller sample of ECoG data).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the approach, with reference to a similar previous study.

claim: In the model used by Zhang et al., anterior-to-posterior increases in theta and beta peak frequencies would correspond to travelling waves from anterior to posterior brain areas.
source: In the model used by Zhang et al. this would correspond to travelling waves from anterior to posterior brain areas (Zhang et al., 2018) that might represent frequency channels for top-down effects (Michalareas et al., 2016; Wang, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the model from Zhang et al., supported by citations.

claim: Anterior-to-posterior travelling waves might represent frequency channels for top-down effects.
source: In the model used by Zhang et al. this would correspond to travelling waves from anterior to posterior brain areas (Zhang et al., 2018) that might represent frequency channels for top-down effects (Michalareas et al., 2016; Wang, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: An alternative explanation for the observed posterior-to-anterior or anterior-to-posterior changes of the band-specific PFs may come from the laminar organization of the cortex, where several layers exhibit distinct frequency profiles and thickness patterns.
source: An alternative explanation for the observed posterior-to-anterior or anterior-to-posterior changes of the band-specific PFs may come from the laminar organization of the cortex, where several layers exhibit distinct frequency profiles (Bastos et al., 2018) and thickness patterns (Wagstyl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Wagstyl and colleagues identified both increasing and decreasing gradients of thickness along the posterior-anterior axis for cortical layers, in the somatosensory, auditory, and motor cortex.
source: In particular, similar to our results for the spatial gradients of band-specific PFs, Wagstyl and colleagues (Wagstyl et al., 2020) have identified both increasing and decreasing gradients of thickness along the posterior-anterior axis for cortical layers, in the somatosensory, auditory, and motor cortex (see Figure 6 of Wagstyl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Peak frequencies of cortical areas form a spatial gradient, which follows the global posterior-anterior hierarchy as well as local anatomical hierarchies.
source: In summary, our findings show that peak frequencies of cortical areas form a spatial gradient, which follows the global posterior-anterior hierarchy as well as local anatomical hierarchies.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from all the experimental results.

claim: The MOUS dataset contains five minutes of resting state MEG recordings available for 197 out of 204 healthy participants.
source: In this study, we used the MOUS dataset (Schoffelen et al., 2019) (https://data.donders.ru.nl/collections/di/dccn/DSC_3011020.09_236?1) which, among others, contains five minutes of resting state MEG recordings that is available for 197 out of a total of 204 healthy participants (age: mean = 22, range = 18–32, gender: 94 females).
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: After removing 10 participants containing excessive artifacts or lacking visible spectral peaks, 187 participants were used for analyses.
source: After removing 10 participants containing excessive ocular-, muscular-, and cardiac-related artefacts, or lacking any visible spectral peak in source space, we used 187 participants for our analyses.
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing and participant selection.

claim: The cortex was parceled to 384 regions-of-interest (ROIs) using the cortical parcellation constructed from the Conte69 atlas.
source: We parceled the cortex to 384 regions-of-interest (ROIs) using the cortical parcellation (introduced in Schoffelen et al., 2017) constructed from the Conte69 atlas (Van Essen et al., 2012), which divides the cortical surface according to the division introduced by Brodmann, 1909.
evidence: This describes the parcellation method used in the study.

claim: The cortical parcellation divides the cortical surface according to the division introduced by Brodmann, 1909.
source: We parceled the cortex to 384 regions-of-interest (ROIs) using the cortical parcellation (introduced in Schoffelen et al., 2017) constructed from the Conte69 atlas (Van Essen et al., 2012), which divides the cortical surface according to the division introduced by Brodmann, 1909.
evidence: This describes the basis of the parcellation scheme.
